title: not "maybe"
tomorrow: plainly, in one session, as a shape not a checklist

segments.voice: Yesterday: alhamdulillah. Praise, whatever the day did. What did you find to praise last night? A small one counts. Day four.

See you tomorrow? Inshallah. Will the report be done by Friday? Inshallah. Are we going to the beach this summer? Inshallah. If you've spent time around Muslim families, you know the joke, and Muslims tell it about themselves: inshallah is the politest way to say probably not. Kids learn early to hear the difference between yes and inshallah. It's a good joke. But it's a joke about how people use the word. The word itself is doing something else, something much older and much more serious about tomorrow.
screen: `SEE YOU TOMORROW? INSHALLAH.` → `THE FAMILY JOKE: PROBABLY NOT.` → `THE WORD MEANS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: In sha' Allah. In: if. Sha'a: wills. Allah: God. If God wills. It comes straight from the Qur'an, from the eighteenth surah, called the Cave. Pickthall's translation reads: “And say not of anything: Lo! I shall do that tomorrow,” and the next verse goes on, “Except if Allah will.” Then it adds: remember your Lord when you forget. Early biographies of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tell a story about these verses: that he was asked some hard questions, promised the answers for the next day without adding if God wills, and the revelation he was waiting for was delayed. Historians treat that as a report from those early biographies, not as settled fact. The verses themselves are plain. So inshallah isn't maybe. Maybe is about your mood. Inshallah is about what you don't control. You can intend something completely, plan it to the minute, and still admit that tomorrow isn't yours to hand out. And it was never meant as a reason to skip the work. There's a well-known hadith in al-Tirmidhi's collection: a man asks the Prophet whether he should leave his camel untied and trust God, or tie it up and trust God. The answer: tie it, and trust. Plan. Show up. Do your part completely. Then say inshallah and mean it: I'm doing what's mine to do, and I know I'm not in charge of the whole of it. People who live by the word say it makes a promise more honest, not less. And it makes a plan that falls through a little easier to forgive.
screen: `IF GOD WILLS.` · `SAY NOT: I SHALL DO THAT TOMORROW.` · `MAYBE IS A MOOD. THIS ISN'T.` · `TIE YOUR CAMEL, AND TRUST.` · then, large: `INSHALLAH.`

segments.voice: Three breaths, with the bell. Think of one thing you've planned for tomorrow, big or small. First breath: see it, the way you intend it to go. Second breath: notice the part of it that's actually up to you. Third breath: notice the part that isn't, and let it be not yours. If you want, on that last breath: inshallah.
Inshallah. If God wills. Not a maybe: a whole plan, held with an open hand. Fourth word.
Your line: if it's meant. Today, when you make a plan with someone, do your part of it completely, and hold the rest a little more loosely. Day four.

screen: `DAY 4 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A SHAPE, NOT A CHECKLIST.`

howItsDone: Muslims add inshallah, "if God wills," whenever they speak of something they intend to do in the future, from meeting a friend tomorrow to a plan years away, following Qur'an 18:23–24.

original.note: Arabic: "if God wills." in (if) + sha'a (wills) + Allah (God), from Qur'an 18:23–24.

trapdoor: what you thought: maybe, or probably not.
what it means: if God wills — a real plan, held with humility about tomorrow.

what a scholar hears: Qur'an 18:23–24 asks that no one say "I shall do that tomorrow" without "except if Allah will." early biographies tie the verses to answers the Prophet promised for the next day; historians treat that as a report, not settled.
